vignette:
When the therapist first meets Mariana, she arrives exactly on time, carrying a heavy toolbox in one hand and a thermos of coffee in the other. The deep calluses on her palms and the grease stains under her nails tell the story of her work before she speaks a word. She is twenty-seven, a licensed HVAC technician for a commercial company in the city, and she lives alone in a small apartment with two cats.

She begins by talking about her job—the crawl spaces, the rooftop units, the sudden blast of a furnace kicking on. It is the only part of her life she can discuss without her voice dropping to a near whisper. But over several sessions, the story beneath the story emerges.

Five years ago, Mariana lived in a small town in Central America. She had just finished technical school and was working for a local refrigeration company. One evening, after repairing a unit at a small grocery store, she was stopped at a makeshift checkpoint. Armed men—members of a local gang that controlled the area—pulled her from her van. They accused her of being an informant for the police. For three days, they held her in a concrete room with no windows. They beat her with pipes, burned her with cigarettes, and repeatedly threatened to kill her. They also sexually assaulted her, though she speaks of this part only in fragments, looking at the floor, her hands pressed flat against her thighs.

After the third day, a neighbor who worked for the local government managed to bribe her release. Mariana fled the country within a week, crossing into the United States as an asylum seeker. She has not seen her family since. She does not know if they are safe.

Now, in her present life, the past is never far. At work, she avoids small, enclosed spaces if possible—though the job often demands them. When she must crawl into an attic or squash herself behind a boiler, her heart pounds so hard she feels it in her throat. She has learned to talk herself through it: It’s just a space. You can leave. The door is open. But the smell of concrete dust or a certain metallic tang can send her back to that room, and she will freeze, unable to move, until a coworker’s voice breaks the spell.

Sudden loud sounds are the worst. The roar of a furnace igniting, the bang of a metal panel falling—she will flinch, drop her tools, and for a moment see the flash of a pipe swinging toward her face. She has started wearing noise-cancelling earbuds on the job, even though it makes communication difficult. Her boss noticed and asked if she was okay. She said it was for tinnitus.

She does not date. The thought of intimacy terrifies her—being touched without warning, being held down, even by accident. At night, she wakes screaming from dreams where she is back in that room, or from dreams where the men have followed her across the border. She keeps her apartment door locked with two deadbolts and a chain, and still she checks it three times before sleep.

The cats help. They sleep on her chest, their weight grounding her. When a car backfires outside, she counts their breaths until her own slows down.

In session, Mariana speaks slowly, choosing each word carefully. She does not cry, but her eyes often go distant. She says she feels hollow, like the real her is somewhere else. She has stopped going to the gym, stopped calling the one friend she made here. She is afraid that if she lets herself feel the anger or the grief, she will never stop.

And yet, every morning, she puts on her work boots, loads her van with equipment, and drives to the next job. She repairs furnaces. She tests airflow. She makes things work again.
